idiom_name: Map<string, Symbol> per scope + parent link
implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits JavaScript's stance - the runtime engine owns lexical environments - so for a compiler, interpreter or linter you build the table yourself: a Map<string, Symbol> per scope with a parent link, define checking has for duplicates and lookup walking outward, plus a discriminated union for symbol kinds because interfaces and type aliases are erased at runtime. What replaces the classic structure is Map plus structural typing: no SymbolTable class hierarchy is required, and the TypeScript compiler's own design is the same shape at scale - the binder creates a SymbolTable per container with a container chain and merges flags for declaration merging, and the checker exposes the result through getSymbolAtLocation and getSymbolsInScope. Keep the hand-rolled chain for your language or DSL; when the code being analysed is TypeScript itself, the checker API is the second variant.
pitfalls: Map keys compare by SameValueZero on strings, but identifiers can arrive with Unicode escapes from the scanner - normalise once, or two spellings of the same name become two symbols.

Type-only declarations vanish at runtime: symbol kinds must be carried as data on the entry (never inferred from a runtime AST shape), and types versus namespaces need separate slots exactly as the compiler merges flags.
Declaration merging means one name may have several declarations: a table that overwrites on duplicate loses the merge and reports a redeclaration where the language allows one.

variants.name: TypeScript compiler checker API
variants.implementation_notes: For TypeScript source the compiler ships the resolved model: after binding, TypeChecker.getSymbolAtLocation(node) returns the symbol a use denotes, getSymbolsInScope(node, flags) lists the symbols visible at a location (the same question a scope table answers), and getTypeAtLocation gives the type - all produced by the binder's internal SymbolTable/container chain, which also handles declaration merging across files and namespaces. What replaces the classic structure is the public compiler API (ts.createProgram plus program.getTypeChecker()). The trade-offs are a heavyweight dependency on the typescript package, resolution that is positional and lazy, and the fact that only TypeScript/JavaScript are resolved, so custom languages still need the Map-based variant.
pitfalls: The checker is lazy and positional: getSymbolsInScope answers for a node in one program state, so results are only comparable within a single Program - rebuild after each edit rather than caching symbols across versions.

getSymbolAtLocation returns undefined for non-identifier nodes and returns aliases for imports: follow checker.getAliasedSymbol before comparing, or the same declaration looks like two different symbols.
